newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM on tiptoe over trade in Clinton summit.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM on tiptoe over trade in Clinton summit.

text.p: Japan will seek to avert a potential flare-up in trade friction with the United States when Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto meets President Bill Clinton on Friday.

Experts said the task is not easy as Japan's contentious current account surplus is set for a series of sharp rises and Hashimoto may not want to do what the United States is urging, namely to loosen his policy of fiscal reform.

"With the next presidential election for his ruling Liberal Democratic Party coming up at the end of September, Hashimoto can in no way moderate his fiscal reform plans until September," said Mitsubishi Research Institute chief economist Johsen Takahashi.
Hashimoto will win a second two-year term as prime minister if he succeeds in retaining the party's presidency.
A Japanese daily said on Wednesday its poll showed that the approval rating for Hashimoto's cabinet fell five percentage points to 34 percent from four months ago.
The U.S. has repeatedly called on Japan not to depend on stepped-up exports to fuel faster growth and instead to enliven domestic demand so as to absorb more imports.
In a letter delivered to Hashimoto in early April, Clinton expressed concern about the Japanese economy and an increase in Japan's trade surplus.
"Japan will tell the U.S. that its current account surplus is most unlikely to rise substantially from mid- and long-term perspectives," a senior Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.

Japan's current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- rose 15.4 percent to $6.92 billion in February from a year earlier, rising for the second month in a row. The January rise was the first in 17 months.
In the letter, Clinton urged Japan to slow the pace of fiscal reforms in case the economy becomes sluggish and Japan's trade surplus rises.
Washington fears that a budget squeeze by Japan, including the April 1 increase in its sales tax, will sap its demand for foreign products.
Japanese and U.S. officials said they do not expect the trade issue to dominate the summit.
Japan rather wants the summit to promote strengthening of bilateral security ties.

Strains arising from the U.S. troop presence in Japan have eased since a new security agreement was signed last year, and Japan last week enacted a law to extend leases on land for U.S. military bases on the island of Okinawa.
Japan also wants the summit to be a venue for exchange of opinions on world affairs such as the situation in the Korean peninsula and aid to poverty-stricken African nations.

"Both sides want to make sure they are giving the right message about continuing their cooperative relations, which have always been good. Hashimoto needs Clinton as part of his political strategy," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
Japanese officials hope the summit will reinforce ties with the United States, which have been the core of Tokyo's diplomacy since the end of World War Two.

"Hashimoto and Clinton have met five times so far. But since this is going to be prime minister's first trip to Washington, and his first meeting with Clinton since the president's second term began, we take the trip very seriously," the Foreign Ministry official said.
During his two-day visit, Hashimoto is also expected to confer with congressional leaders and Vice President Al Gore. He will visit Australia and New Zealand before returning home.
